name: Design a Model Registry and Serving Platform
intent: Let teams publish trained models as immutable, traceable versions and turn them into live endpoints that are promoted through gates, rolled out gradually, scaled with demand (even from zero) and rolled back in seconds.
codeTitle: a model registry with gates, rollback and a canary split
finalIntro: One new model version going from upload to live traffic.
prompt: Design an internal platform where 200 teams publish trained models and deploy them as endpoints. Each model version must be reproducible and traceable to its code, data and hyperparameters, promoted to production only after evaluation and approval, rolled out to live traffic gradually, scaled on demand including down to zero, and rolled back quickly. Some weights are tens of gigabytes and the GPUs are expensive.
functional: Publish a trained model as a new immutable version, with its lineage: code commit, training data snapshot, hyperparameters and metrics
Move a version through stages (staging, production) with evaluation gates and an approval
Package a version into a serving image and deploy it as an endpoint
Roll out with a canary, shadow traffic or blue-green, and split traffic between versions
Autoscale replicas on queue depth or GPU load, including scale to zero and back
Roll back to the previous version quickly
Show metrics per version and run drift checks
Control who can publish, approve and deploy, and keep an audit trail
nonFunctional: A published version can never change, and a corrupted download is always detected
Rollback takes seconds, because the previous version is still warm
A cold replica serves its first request in under about 15 seconds, even for a 14 GB model
Packing several small models on one GPU must not let one model starve another
Every production change can be traced to a person, an approval and the evaluation that allowed it
Hundreds of endpoints and thousands of versions, with registry reads in tens of milliseconds

firstAttempt.text: Teams copy a weights file into a shared storage bucket named model_final_v2_REALLY_FINAL.pt, and an engineer copies it to a GPU machine by hand and restarts the server. Which version is live is written in a chat message.
limits: Files can be overwritten, so nobody can say what exactly was serving last Tuesday
Nothing records which code, data and settings produced the weights, so a result cannot be reproduced
There is no gate, so an untested model can reach production because one person was in a hurry
A restart drops traffic, and rollback means finding and copying the old file again
Each GPU machine runs one model, so most of the expensive hardware sits idle
Nobody can tell who changed what, or notice that a model has quietly got worse

steps.title: Store every model as an immutable, checksummed version
steps.problem: A file in a bucket can be overwritten, and without a record of how it was made, nobody can reproduce it, trust it or explain it.
steps.fix: Publishing goes through a registry API. The weights are uploaded to an artifact store addressed by their content hash, and the registry records a new numbered version in a metadata database: the hash, the code commit, the training data snapshot, the hyperparameters, the training metrics and the author. Versions are write-once. Uploading identical bytes again returns the existing version, and every download is verified against the stored checksum. Big files are uploaded in resumable chunks.
steps.tradeoff: Any version can be fetched, reproduced and compared exactly, and corruption or tampering is detected. Storage grows with every version, so old versions need a retention rule, and lineage is only as good as the training code that reports it honestly.

steps.title: Promote through stages with evaluation gates and approval
steps.problem: If anyone can point production at any version, an untested or slower model reaches users, and nobody knows who allowed it.
steps.fix: A version starts with no stage. Moving it to staging triggers evaluation jobs: accuracy on a held-out set, slices that matter such as new users or rare classes, latency and memory on the real hardware, and a bias or safety check. The gates compare the result with the current production version, for example accuracy no more than 0.5 points lower and p95 latency under 120 ms. Production needs a second person who is not the author to approve, and every transition writes an audit record with who, when, which evaluation and which version it replaced. Roles control who can publish, approve and deploy to each environment.
steps.tradeoff: Bad models are stopped before users see them, and each production change has a named owner. Gates can be too strict or too loose, offline evaluation never fully predicts live behaviour, and approvals slow urgent fixes, so there is an emergency path that is loud and audited.

steps.title: Package a version into a serving image
steps.problem: A weights file alone cannot answer requests, and the runtime, library versions and preprocessing must match what the model was evaluated with.
steps.fix: When a version is approved, a builder produces a serving image from a pinned base, the inference runtime, the pre- and post-processing code and the model's signature. The image is scanned, signed, and recorded against the version. The weights are not baked into the image when they are large: the image stays small and the server fetches the weights by hash at start-up, then keeps them in a per-node cache. Small models can be packed several to a GPU, each with a memory limit and a share of compute, so a single card is not idle.
steps.tradeoff: The thing that was evaluated is exactly the thing that runs, and images stay small and fast to pull. Packing raises GPU use but makes models share memory and cache, so one hungry model can hurt its neighbours unless limits are enforced.

steps.title: Roll out with a traffic split, and keep the old version warm
steps.problem: Switching all traffic to a new model at once means a regression that offline tests missed hits every user, and rolling back is slow if the old version was shut down.
steps.fix: A router in front of the endpoint sends each request to a version according to weights. Shadow mode copies requests to the new version and discards its answers, to compare outputs safely. A canary sends a small share, such as 5 percent, chosen by hashing the request or user id so the same caller keeps the same version, and steps up to 25, 50 and 100 while per-version error rate, latency and a quality signal stay within bounds. Blue-green keeps both fleets and flips a pointer. The previous version stays loaded until the new one has been stable for a while, so rollback is moving the weights back, not redeploying.
steps.tradeoff: A bad model harms a few callers briefly, and rollback takes seconds. Running two versions costs extra GPUs for a while, and comparing versions fairly needs enough traffic and a sticky split.

steps.title: Autoscale on queue depth, including from zero
steps.problem: GPUs are expensive to leave idle, but a model with no replicas has nothing to answer the first request, and a 14 GB model takes a long time to load.
steps.fix: The autoscaler watches the request queue depth and in-flight requests per replica, which exist even at zero replicas, and not GPU utilisation alone, which cannot be measured when nothing is running and lags behind a burst. Desired replicas follow the backlog, with a stabilisation window before scaling down. For scale from zero the platform keeps cold starts short: weights are pre-pulled to node disks or a shared read-only volume, loaded from local NVMe rather than a remote store, and critical endpoints keep a minimum of one replica. Requests wait in a bounded queue with a deadline while a replica starts. Model servers use continuous batching so one replica serves many requests.
steps.tradeoff: Cost follows demand and a burst finds capacity quickly. A cold start is still a delay of seconds, a minimum replica costs money all day, and caches on every node cost disk.

steps.title: Watch each version and detect drift
steps.problem: A model can pass every gate and still get worse in production as the data it sees changes, and an aggregate dashboard hides which version is to blame.
steps.fix: Every request is labelled with the endpoint, model version and image, so latency, error rate, queue time, GPU use and output distributions are recorded per version. Sampled inputs and predictions are stored, to compare with the training data and, once labels arrive, with the truth. Drift hooks compute input and prediction distribution shifts and raise an alert, or start a retrain or a rollback, when a threshold is crossed. Metrics use bounded labels, so cardinality stays small, and a version page in the registry shows the lineage, the gate results and the live health in one place.
steps.tradeoff: Quality problems are noticed in hours rather than at the next quarterly review, and blame points to one version. Drift is a signal and not a proof, so thresholds create false alarms, and ground truth can arrive weeks late.

failures.scenario: A weights download is cut off or corrupted
failures.impact: A replica could load a truncated file and serve nonsense, or crash in a loop.
failures.answer: The server hashes the file against the registry checksum before loading and refuses to start on a mismatch. It retries the download, resuming from where it stopped, with backoff, and the node cache stores only verified files. The replica never reports ready until verification passes.

failures.scenario: A canary passes every offline gate and then performs badly on live traffic
failures.impact: Five percent of callers get worse answers, which no latency alert notices.
failures.answer: The rollout compares the canary with the stable version on the same live traffic, including a quality signal and the output distribution. When the difference passes a threshold the router returns to 0 percent automatically, and the stable version is still warm so it takes effect in seconds. The incident is attached to the version in the registry.

failures.scenario: A burst hits an endpoint that has scaled to zero
failures.impact: Requests pile up while the first replicas load 14 GB of weights, and many time out.
failures.answer: Requests wait in a bounded queue with a deadline, and the queue depth itself triggers scaling, so replicas start at the first request. Pre-pulled weights on node disks cut the load from tens of seconds to about ten. Excess requests beyond the queue limit are rejected quickly instead of piling up, and endpoints with strict latency keep a minimum replica.

failures.scenario: Packed models fight over one GPU
failures.impact: One model's large batch uses the card's memory, and a neighbour fails with out-of-memory or slows down.
failures.answer: Each packed model gets a fixed memory budget and a compute share, enforced by the runtime or by hardware partitioning, and the scheduler packs only models whose measured peaks fit. Busy or latency-critical models get their own card. Per-model GPU memory and queue time are watched, so a noisy neighbour is moved before it hurts.

failures.scenario: Many nodes download the same weights at once after a failure
failures.impact: The artifact store's bandwidth is shared out, so every cold start takes several times longer.
failures.answer: Nodes fetch from a regional mirror or a shared read-only volume, and a node that already has the file serves it to its neighbours. The autoscaler staggers starts instead of launching everything together, and the weights of live models are kept pre-pulled, so a recovery does not depend on one store.

alternatives.title: How weights reach a new replica

options.name: Bake the weights into the image
options.pro: One artifact to pull, and it is simple
options.con: Images of tens of gigabytes are slow to build and pull, and every model change rebuilds everything

options.name: Download from the artifact store at start-up
options.pro: Small images, and weights are verified by hash
options.con: Slow cold starts, and all nodes share the store's bandwidth

options.name: Local disk or shared volume cache
options.pro: Fast cold starts, with a few seconds to load
options.con: Cache management, disk cost and invalidation

alternatives.pick: Small images, weights fetched by hash into a per-node cache that is pre-pulled for live models.

alternatives.title: How to roll out a new version

options.name: Shadow
options.pro: No user impact, and outputs can be compared
options.con: Doubles compute, and cannot show how users react

options.name: Canary with a sticky split
options.con: Needs enough traffic and good comparison metrics

options.name: Blue-green
options.con: Needs a whole second fleet of GPUs

alternatives.pick: Shadow for risky changes, then a canary. Blue-green when a clean switch matters more than the cost.

alternatives.title: What the autoscaler watches

options.name: GPU or CPU utilisation
options.con: Cannot see demand at zero replicas, and reacts after the burst has arrived

options.name: Queue depth and in-flight requests
options.pro: Leads the load and works from zero
options.con: Needs a queue and tuning per model

options.name: A schedule or a forecast
options.pro: Capacity is ready before the daily peak
options.con: Wrong on unusual days, so it is only an addition

alternatives.pick: Queue depth as the main signal, with a schedule for predictable peaks.

alternatives.title: How to share a GPU between models

options.name: One model per GPU
options.con: Wastes cards on small or quiet models

options.name: Time-slicing or process sharing
options.pro: Easy to turn on, and flexible
options.con: No memory isolation, so noisy neighbours

options.name: Hardware partitions
options.con: Fixed sizes, and only on supported cards

alternatives.pick: Hardware partitions or strict memory budgets for small models, and a dedicated card for big or critical ones.

roles.description: Evaluation runs that gate each promotion.

quiz.question: Teams copy weights into a shared bucket under names like model_final_v2.pt, and retraining overwrites the file. A customer complains about answers from last Tuesday, but nobody can say which weights served then, or which code and data produced them. What change fixes this at the root?
options: Turn on object versioning for the bucket and require a date suffix on every file name, so each overwrite keeps the old file
Keep a shared wiki page where each engineer lists the commit and the dataset used for every model they upload
Copy each model to a second bucket every night, and keep the nightly copies for 90 days as the record of what ran
Publish through a registry that stores weights by content hash as write-once versions, with commit, data and settings
quiz.explanation: A write-once version in a registry ties the exact bytes, by hash, to the code, data and settings that made them, so Tuesday's model can be fetched and reproduced. Bucket versioning and nightly copies keep old files but say nothing about how they were made, and a wiki page depends on people remembering to update it.

quiz.question: A 14 GB model must serve its first request within 15 seconds of a cold start. Weights come from a remote artifact store with 10 Gbps (about 1.25 GB/s) of total egress shared by all nodes. A zone failure makes 10 nodes start replicas of this model at once. Which change meets the target?
options: Double the artifact store's egress to 20 Gbps, which halves the download time for each starting node
Bake the 14 GB weights into the serving image, so that one image pull replaces the separate weights download
Keep live models' weights pre-pulled on node-local NVMe, and load them from there
Lengthen the autoscaler's stabilisation window to 10 minutes, so that replicas are started less often
quiz.explanation: Ten nodes sharing 1.25 GB/s each get about 0.125 GB/s, so 14 GB takes around 112 seconds, and doubling egress still leaves about 56. Local pre-pulled weights avoid the shared link altogether. A baked image is still pulled over a shared link, and a longer window does not make any single start faster.

quiz.question: One 80 GB GPU hosts three small models that peak at 10, 12 and 8 GB. Time-slicing is on, with no memory limits. Once a day the 12 GB model receives a large batch and takes about 45 GB, and its neighbours crash with out-of-memory errors. What is the best fix?
options: Keep time-slicing and add a retry with backoff to the two neighbours, so they come back once the large batch has finished
Give each packed model a fixed memory budget and compute share, and move the spiky model to a card of its own
Stop packing, and run every model, including the quiet small ones, on its own dedicated GPU from now on
Raise the batch timeout on the spiky model, so its large batches are split into several smaller ones over time
quiz.explanation: Time-slicing shares compute but gives no memory isolation, so budgets enforced by the runtime or hardware partitions are needed, and a model with a large measured peak does not fit a shared slot. One model per GPU does work but wastes cards on quiet models, and retries only hide the crashes.
